subject_entity.notes: Deacon of Cyprian of Carthage; accompanied Cyprian into exile and was present at his martyrdom in 258; author of the Vita Cypriani, the earliest Latin Christian biography; provides key details about Cyprian's conversion, episcopate, and death.

object_entity.notes: Cyprian of Carthage was arrested, tried before the proconsul Galerius Maximus, and beheaded on September 14, 258 during the Valerianic persecution; the Acta Proconsularia preserve the trial proceedings; Pontius the Deacon wrote the earliest Latin Christian biography (Vita Cypriani) describing his death; Cyprian was the first African bishop to be martyred.

context_place.notes: Major North African city; center of Latin Christianity from Tertullian through Cyprian and Augustine; seat of important regional councils.

evidence.notes: Pontius was present at Cyprian's martyrdom per Eusebius.

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: Eusebius records that Cyprian was banished under the Emperor Valerian and thereafter summoned back only to be executed. Pontius the deacon, who was with him, wrote an account of his life and death.
passage.notes: Cyprian's exile and martyrdom under Valerian; Pontius as witness and biographer

subject_entity.notes: Novatian, a Roman presbyter, set himself up as rival bishop of Rome c. 251 in opposition to Pope Cornelius; refused readmission of Christians who had lapsed during the Decian persecution; condemned by a Roman synod; his followers formed the Novatianist sect which spread across the empire.

evidence.notes: The schism occurred c. 251.

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: Eusebius reports that Hippolytus was a bishop somewhere and that he composed various works. In HE 6.43, Eusebius preserves a letter of Cornelius of Rome describing Novatian's ordination as rival bishop and the condemnation of his rigorist position by a Roman synod of sixty bishops.
passage.notes: Eusebius testimony to Hippolytus's episcopacy and works; Cornelius's letter on Novatian schism; Roman synod against Novatian

object_entity.notes: Systematic persecution of Christians in the Sasanian Empire beginning c. 340 under Shapur II; motivated partly by Constantine's declaration of Rome as a Christian empire; Aphrahat wrote his later Demonstrations during this crisis; lasted intermittently until Shapur's death in 379.

evidence.notes: Aphrahat addresses Christians under Shapur II's persecution.

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: Aphrahat addresses the Christians suffering under Shapur II's persecution; he encourages steadfastness, reminding them that persecution purifies the church; the martyrs receive a crown; God will vindicate his people as he did Israel in Egypt.
passage.notes: On Persecution under Shapur II

subject_entity.notes: First ecumenical council convened by Emperor Constantine at Nicaea in Bithynia, May–August 325 CE. Addressed the Arian controversy; produced the original Nicene Creed affirming the Son as homoousios (same substance) with the Father; condemned Arius; standardized Easter dating; addressed the Meletian schism in Egypt. Attended by ~300 bishops, mostly from the East. Jacob of Nisibis and Eusebius of Caesarea were among the attendees.

object_entity.notes: Ancient city in Bithynia (modern İznik, Turkey); site of the First Ecumenical Council (325 CE) and Second Ecumenical Council (787 CE).

passage.excerpt: Constantine convened the universal synod at Nicaea in Bithynia, gathering bishops from all regions of the empire.
passage.notes: Vita Constantini 3.6-14; primary narrative source for Nicaea.

object_entity.description: The Aksumite kingdom (Ethiopia) received Christianity through the mission of Frumentius, consecrated by Athanasius of Alexandria, who converted King Ezana c. 330; attested by Rufinus, Socrates, Sozomen.

evidence.notes: Philostorgius HE 3.4 describes Theophilus's mission to Ethiopia (Himyar/Axum region).

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: Theophilus called the Indian was sent by Emperor Constantius on an embassy to the Himyarites in south Arabia. He was originally from the island of Dibus (Socotra). He converted the Himyarites and built three churches: one in Zafar the capital, one in Aden, and one near the Persian Gulf. He also visited the Aksumites and corrected their worship.
passage.notes: Key source for Arabian/Himyarite Christianity and Theophilus's mission; preserved in Photius's epitome.

subject_entity.notes: Frumentius consecrated bishop by Athanasius and returns to Aksum c. 328–333; King Ezana converts; Christianity becomes state religion of the Aksumite Empire.

object_entity.notes: Capital of the Aksumite Empire; site of Frumentius's episcopal see; Christianity became state religion under King Ezana c. 330; major Red Sea trade hub.

evidence.notes: Rufinus locates the event at Aksum.

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: A philosopher named Meropius of Tyre sailed to India with two boys Frumentius and Aedesius. The ship was seized and all killed except the boys who were brought to the king of Aksum. When the king died the queen asked Frumentius to help govern. Frumentius sought out Roman traders who were Christians and built churches. Later he traveled to Alexandria where Athanasius consecrated him bishop. He returned to Aksum and converted many including the king.
passage.notes: Primary Western source for the christianization of Aksum; Rufinus heard the account from Aedesius himself.

subject_entity.notes: Conversion of King Abgar VIII of Osroene to Christianity c. 200 AD, making Edessa likely the first Christian state; the historical kernel behind the later legendary Abgar-Jesus correspondence in Eusebius HE 1.13.

object_entity.notes: Capital of Osroene in upper Mesopotamia; spiritual capital of Syriac Christianity; home of Bardaisan, Ephrem (after 363), and the Abgar/Addai tradition; site of the School of the Persians.

evidence.notes: Conversion narrative set in Edessa.

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: Eusebius reproduces documents from the archives of Edessa: King Abgar writes to Jesus asking for healing; Jesus replies promising to send a disciple after his ascension; Thomas later sends Thaddaeus (Addai) who heals Abgar and evangelizes Edessa.
passage.notes: Abgar-Jesus correspondence and Addai tradition
